# Sample Size for a Single Mean {#sec-single-mean}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Identify expected SD and precision in the same units.
- Compute a one-sample mean precision requirement.
:::

## The idea

For a mean estimated from independent observations, a common approximate planning expression depends on the expected standard deviation $\sigma$, normal critical value and desired confidence-interval half-width $d$. The SD expresses outcome dispersion; precision expresses tolerated uncertainty in the estimated mean. These are different quantities but must have the same units.

## When and how to apply it

A small pilot may yield an unstable SD. Sensitivity analysis over plausible SDs provides a more defensible design than selecting the smallest reported value. Normal planning is not an exact small-sample t-based assurance procedure.

## Formula at a glance

$$
n_0=\frac{Z_{1-\alpha/2}^2\sigma^2}{d^2}
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
To estimate mean haemoglobin with SD 10 g/L and half-width 2 g/L at 95% confidence, $n_0=1.96^2(10)^2/2^2=96.04$. Therefore, plan **97 complete observations**.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Calculation logic

The example uses the stated planning assumptions and mathematical approximation. Explain why they apply before reporting the numerical result.

### Copy-and-run R

```r
sd <- 10; d <- 2
ceiling(qnorm(.975)^2 * sd^2 / d^2)
```

:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Do not confuse a sample mean, SD, SE and confidence-interval width.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Compare the requirements when the anticipated SD increases from 10 to 15 g/L at the same precision.
